name: RCP 201 Quick Answers
source: RCP 201 Quick Answers study guide (slides + Whitaker 4th ed.)

cards.q: What are the 3 prenatal stages and how long does each last?
cards.a:
What are the 3 prenatal stages and how long does each last?
Ovum 12–14 days → embryo 54–56 days (ends at 3 cm crown–rump) → fetus 210–214 days
(40 weeks, 3 trimesters)

cards.q: Define neonate, infant and child by age.
cards.a:
Define neonate, infant and child by age.
Neonate: birth to 1 month
Infant: 1 month to 1 year
Child: over 1 year

cards.q: List the 5 stages of fetal lung development with their weeks.
cards.a:
List the 5 stages of fetal lung development with their weeks.
Embryonal (to wk 7) → pseudoglandular (7–16) → canalicular (17–26) → saccular (26–36) → alveolar (true alveoli 32–34 wk, increasing to age 8)

cards.q: When does the lung bud appear?
cards.a:
When does the lung bud appear?
Day 24 (embryonal stage)

cards.q: When does gas exchange first become possible?
cards.a:
When does gas exchange first become possible?
24–25 weeks — in the canalicular stage, when vessels form.

cards.q: What happens in the pseudoglandular stage?
cards.a:
What happens in the pseudoglandular stage?
Weeks 7–16: the airways branch and the lung looks like a gland.

cards.q: What happens in the canalicular stage?
cards.a:
What happens in the canalicular stage?
Weeks 17–26: bronchioles multiply, vessels form, and alveoli begin.

cards.q: What happens in the saccular stage?
cards.a:
What happens in the saccular stage?
Weeks 26–36: alveoli develop (lungs formed by 24–26 wk).

cards.q: By what week is the fetal heart fully formed?
cards.a:
By what week is the fetal heart fully formed?
Week 8

cards.q: Term vs premature — the cutoff?
cards.a:
Term vs premature — the cutoff?
Term > 37 weeks; premature < 37 weeks.

cards.q: What is Nägele's rule?
cards.a:
What is Nägele's rule?
Due date = LMP − 3 months + 7 days.

cards.q: Besides Nägele's rule, what else dates a pregnancy — and when do quickening and heart tones appear?
cards.a:
Besides Nägele's rule, what else dates a pregnancy — and when do quickening and heart tones appear?
Fundal height, quickening (16–22 wk) and heart tones (16–20 wk).

cards.q: After birth, how is gestational age scored, and how is size classed?
cards.a:
After birth, how is gestational age scored, and how is size classed?
Scored by Dubowitz or Ballard. Classed as AGA (10th–90th percentile), SGA (< 10th) or LGA (> 90th).

cards.q: Embryonal lung stage — slides vs Whitaker: how long does it last?
cards.a:
Embryonal lung stage — slides vs Whitaker: how long does it last?
Slides: the first 7 weeks. Whitaker: 8.

cards.q: When do alveoli begin forming, and when do true alveoli appear?
cards.a:
When do alveoli begin forming, and when do true alveoli appear?
Begin in the canalicular stage (17–26 wk), keep developing in the saccular stage (26–36 wk). True alveoli at 32–34 weeks.

cards.q: How many alveoli at birth, and until what age does the number increase?
cards.a:
How many alveoli at birth, and until what age does the number increase?
50–150 million at birth, increasing until about age 8.

cards.q: Why don't small alveoli collapse?
cards.a:
Why don't small alveoli collapse?
Surfactant lines them and lowers surface tension (Laplace).

cards.q: What is surfactant, what does it do, and which cells make it?
cards.a:
What is surfactant, what does it do, and which cells make it?
A substance on the alveolar wall that lowers surface tension, keeps alveoli open and reduces the work of breathing. Made by type II cells.

cards.q: What is surfactant made of?
cards.a:
What is surfactant made of?
Phospholipids (mainly DPPC/lecithin), neutral lipids and proteins.

cards.q: When does surfactant production start, and when is it mature? What L/S ratio?
cards.a:
When does surfactant production start, and when is it mature? What L/S ratio?
Starts at 24 weeks; mature at about 35 weeks (L/S ratio 2:1).

cards.q: What disease results from surfactant deficiency, and how is surfactant given?
cards.a:
What disease results from surfactant deficiency, and how is surfactant given?
RDS. Replacement is instilled down the ETT, prophylactically or as rescue therapy.

cards.q: Fetal lung fluid not cleared at birth causes what?
cards.a:
Fetal lung fluid not cleared at birth causes what?
TTN.

cards.q: What is the placenta, and what are its size facts at term?
cards.a:
What is the placenta, and what are its size facts at term?
The fetal organ of respiration. At term it covers ⅓ of the uterus and weighs about 1 lb. Maternal and fetal blood never mix.

cards.q: What is the amnion, and when does it form?
cards.a:
What is the amnion, and when does it form?
The sac surrounding the fetus that holds the amniotic fluid; forms around day 7.

cards.q: What does amniotic fluid do, and what is it sampled for?
cards.a:
What does amniotic fluid do, and what is it sampled for?
Protects the fetus, allows movement, aids thermoregulation; sampled for lung maturity (L/S ratio).

cards.q: Amniotic fluid volume at term — slides vs Whitaker?
cards.a:
Amniotic fluid volume at term — slides vs Whitaker?
Slides: about 1 L. Whitaker: about 600 mL.

cards.q: How many vessels are in the umbilical cord, and what does each carry?
cards.a:
How many vessels are in the umbilical cord, and what does each carry?
3: 2 arteries (back to the placenta) and 1 vein (oxygenated blood to the fetus), in Wharton's jelly.

cards.q: Name the 3 fetal shunts and what each connects.
cards.a:
Name the 3 fetal shunts and what each connects.
Ductus venosus: umbilical vein → IVC (bypasses liver)
Foramen ovale: RA → LA
Ductus arteriosus: pulmonary artery → aorta (bypasses lungs)

cards.q: At birth, what happens to SVR and PVR, and why?
cards.a:
At birth, what happens to SVR and PVR, and why?
Placenta removed → SVR rises. Lungs expand and O₂ dilates them → PVR falls.

cards.q: Why does the foramen ovale close at birth?
cards.a:
Why does the foramen ovale close at birth?
Systemic pressure rises, so left-atrial pressure exceeds right and the flap is pushed shut.

cards.q: How long does the ductus arteriosus take to close, and what if it doesn't?
cards.a:
How long does the ductus arteriosus take to close, and what if it doesn't?
About 96 hours; surgery if it doesn't close.

cards.q: What does each fetal structure become after birth — DA, DV, umbilical vein, umbilical arteries?
cards.a:
What does each fetal structure become after birth — DA, DV, umbilical vein, umbilical arteries?
DA → ligamentum arteriosum
DV → ligamentum venosum
Umbilical vein → ligamentum teres
Umbilical arteries → medial umbilical ligaments

cards.q: What is the foramen ovale and which way does it shunt?
cards.a:
What is the foramen ovale and which way does it shunt?
An opening between the atria that shunts blood right atrium → left atrium, bypassing the lungs.

cards.q: Why does fetal blood cross the foramen ovale right-to-left?
cards.a:
Why does fetal blood cross the foramen ovale right-to-left?
Fetal right-side pressure is higher than left.

cards.q: The foramen ovale fails to close. What is that called?
cards.a:
The foramen ovale fails to close. What is that called?
ASD (atrial septal defect).

cards.q: Umbilical vein vs artery — clinical uses?
cards.a:
Umbilical vein vs artery — clinical uses?
Vein: emergency drug and fluid access
Artery: blood sampling and UAC — thrombus is the most common complication

cards.q: What is Wharton's jelly and what does it do?
cards.a:
What is Wharton's jelly and what does it do?
The tough, gelatinous tissue around the three umbilical vessels. It insulates and protects them and keeps the cord from kinking.

cards.q: After delivery, how fast does Wharton's jelly collapse the cord vessels, and why?
cards.a:
After delivery, how fast does Wharton's jelly collapse the cord vessels, and why?
Within about 5 minutes — triggered by the temperature change.

cards.q: Where are the chemoreceptors and baroreceptors?
cards.a:
Where are the chemoreceptors and baroreceptors?
Chemoreceptors: carotid and aortic bodies
Baroreceptors: carotid bifurcation and aortic arch

cards.q: Pre- vs postductal sampling sites?
cards.a:
Pre- vs postductal sampling sites?
Right radial = preductal; UAC = postductal.

cards.q: Name 4 arterial defects.
cards.a:
Name 4 arterial defects.
Coarctation of the aorta, tetralogy (pulmonary artery obstruction), transposition, truncus arteriosus.

cards.q: Why are fetal pressures reversed (right higher than left)?
cards.a:
Why are fetal pressures reversed (right higher than left)?
The fluid-filled lungs resist flow while the placenta does not.

cards.q: Trace fetal blood from the placenta to the aorta through the foramen ovale.
cards.a:
Trace fetal blood from the placenta to the aorta through the foramen ovale.
Placenta → umbilical vein → ductus venosus → IVC → right atrium → foramen ovale → left heart → aorta

cards.q: What path does the blood take that goes through the ductus arteriosus?
cards.a:
What path does the blood take that goes through the ductus arteriosus?
RV → pulmonary artery → ductus arteriosus → aorta. The umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta.

cards.q: Fetal circulation fails to convert at birth. What is that called?
cards.a:
Fetal circulation fails to convert at birth. What is that called?
PPHN

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: What is tocolysis, how common is premature labor, and when is it used?
cards.a:
What is tocolysis, how common is premature labor, and when is it used?
Stopping premature labor (12% of pregnancies). Used before 37 weeks and with placenta previa.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: Which tocolytics are beta-sympathomimetics, and how do they work?
cards.a:
Which tocolytics are beta-sympathomimetics, and how do they work?
Terbutaline and ritodrine — stimulate β-receptors to relax uterine smooth muscle.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: β-agonist tocolytic side effects — mother, fetus, newborn?
cards.a:
β-agonist tocolytic side effects — mother, fetus, newborn?
Mother: tachycardia, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, pulmonary edema
Fetus: tachycardia
Newborn: rebound hypoglycemia

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: How does magnesium sulfate work as a tocolytic, and what can it do to the newborn?
cards.a:
How does magnesium sulfate work as a tocolytic, and what can it do to the newborn?
Lowers muscle contractility. Newborn may be hypotonic or apneic (hypermagnesemia).

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: Indomethacin and nifedipine — how do they work, and what fetal risk does indomethacin carry?
cards.a:
Indomethacin and nifedipine — how do they work, and what fetal risk does indomethacin carry?
Indomethacin blocks prostaglandins and can constrict the fetal ductus arteriosus. Nifedipine is a calcium-channel blocker.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: What is chorioamnionitis?
cards.a:
What is chorioamnionitis?
Bacterial infection and inflammation of the fetal membranes and amniotic fluid.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: What causes chorioamnionitis, and what membrane-rupture time raises the risk?
cards.a:
What causes chorioamnionitis, and what membrane-rupture time raises the risk?
Organisms ascend the birth canal, especially after membranes have been ruptured > 24 hours.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: Chorioamnionitis: the clue, the neonatal risk, and the treatment?
cards.a:
Chorioamnionitis: the clue, the neonatal risk, and the treatment?
Foul-smelling amniotic fluid and baby. Raises risk of neonatal sepsis and pneumonia. Treat the newborn with broad-spectrum antibiotics.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: Cervical dilation vs effacement — and full dilation?
cards.a:
Cervical dilation vs effacement — and full dilation?
Dilation = widening, in cm; full at 10 cm. Effacement = thinning, in %.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: What are the 3 stages of labor?
cards.a:
What are the 3 stages of labor?
Stage 1: onset of contractions → full dilation
Stage 2: full dilation → delivery
Stage 3: delivery of the placenta

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: What is placenta previa, and what are its 3 types?
cards.a:
What is placenta previa, and what are its 3 types?
Placenta implants low in the uterus, near or over the cervical opening. Types: low (marginal), partial, total (covers the os).

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: How is placenta previa diagnosed, and why is it dangerous?
cards.a:
How is placenta previa diagnosed, and why is it dangerous?
Ultrasound. It blocks fetal passage, risks abruption, is a high-risk pregnancy factor and a cause of fetal asphyxia.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: Indications for cesarean section?
cards.a:
Indications for cesarean section?
Prior cesarean, dystocia (failure to progress), breech, fetal distress — also transverse lie, abruptio placentae, maternal active herpes.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::03 Fetal Assessment, Labor & Delivery
cards.q: What neonatal respiratory risk comes with cesarean delivery?
cards.a:
What neonatal respiratory risk comes with cesarean delivery?
Retained lung fluid → TTN.

cards.q: Define asphyxia, and list its causes.
cards.a:
Define asphyxia, and list its causes.
Hypoxia + hypercapnia + acidosis. Causes: maternal hypoxia, poor placental flow, cord blockage, fetal anemia or drugs.

cards.q: How does fetal asphyxia present in utero?
cards.a:
How does fetal asphyxia present in utero?
Fetal bradycardia (< 100), loss of variability, late decelerations, meconium-stained fluid, low scalp pH (< 7.20 = severe).

cards.q: What is the sequence of events as asphyxia progresses?
cards.a:
What is the sequence of events as asphyxia progresses?
HR and BP fall; primary apnea → weak gasping → secondary apnea.

cards.q: How is fetal asphyxia treated before birth?
cards.a:
How is fetal asphyxia treated before birth?
O₂ to the mother, reposition her (cord compression), amnioinfusion, and rapid delivery (cesarean if needed).

cards.q: After birth, when do you start PPV and when do you add compressions? What ratio?
cards.a:
After birth, when do you start PPV and when do you add compressions? What ratio?
PPV if apneic, gasping, or HR < 100. Compressions if HR < 60 after 30 s of PPV, at 3:1.

cards.q: Neonatal epinephrine and volume doses?
cards.a:
Neonatal epinephrine and volume doses?
Epinephrine 1:10,000, 0.1–0.3 mL/kg IV
Volume 10 mL/kg for blood loss

cards.q: How should you treat every apneic newborn?
cards.a:
How should you treat every apneic newborn?
As if in secondary apnea — ventilate.

cards.q: What are the 5 Apgar signs, and how is it scored and timed?
cards.a:
What are the 5 Apgar signs, and how is it scored and timed?
Heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, color — each 0/1/2 (total 0–10), at 1 and 5 minutes; repeated every 5 min up to 20 min if low.

cards.q: Apgar heart rate: what earns 0, 1, 2?
cards.a:
Apgar heart rate: what earns 0, 1, 2?
0 none · 1 slow/irregular · 2 > 100

cards.q: Apgar respiratory effort: what earns 0, 1, 2?
cards.a:
Apgar respiratory effort: what earns 0, 1, 2?

<hr id=answer>

0 apnea · 1 irregular/gasping · 2 crying

cards.q: Apgar muscle tone: what earns 0, 1, 2?
cards.a:
Apgar muscle tone: what earns 0, 1, 2?

<hr id=answer>

0 flaccid · 1 some flexion · 2 well flexed

cards.q: Apgar reflex irritability: what earns 0, 1, 2?
cards.a:
Apgar reflex irritability: what earns 0, 1, 2?

<hr id=answer>

0 none · 1 grimace · 2 crying

cards.q: Apgar color: what earns 0, 1, 2?
cards.a:
Apgar color: what earns 0, 1, 2?
0 pale/blue · 1 acrocyanosis (pink body, blue hands and feet) · 2 all pink

cards.q: What is the Apgar used for, which score predicts future impairment, and what scores need intervention?
cards.a:
What is the Apgar used for, which score predicts future impairment, and what scores need intervention?
Objectively evaluates the newborn and response to resuscitation. The 5-minute score predicts future impairment. < 6 at 1 min or < 7 at 5 min needs intervention. Never delay resuscitation to score it.

cards.q: Why does meconium get passed and aspirated, and which babies does MAS affect?
cards.a:
Why does meconium get passed and aspirated, and which babies does MAS affect?
Fetal asphyxia increases gut movement and relaxes the anal sphincter; the fetus then gasps it in. Affects term and post-term babies.

cards.q: Signs of meconium aspiration?
cards.a:
Signs of meconium aspiration?
Green-stained amniotic fluid, low Apgar, fetal hypoxia and acidosis, abnormal heart tracings.

cards.q: What lung injuries does meconium cause, and what does the CXR show?
cards.a:
What lung injuries does meconium cause, and what does the CXR show?
Ball-valve air trapping (→ air leaks), chemical pneumonitis, and PPHN. CXR: patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation.

cards.q: Meconium: a non-vigorous baby vs a vigorous baby — what do you do?
cards.a:
Meconium: a non-vigorous baby vs a vigorous baby — what do you do?
Not vigorous (HR < 100, weak effort, poor tone) → intubate and suction the trachea.
Vigorous → bulb-suction mouth and nose.

cards.q: Other MAS treatments besides suctioning?
cards.a:
Other MAS treatments besides suctioning?
Amnioinfusion (warm saline) to dilute · warm humidified O₂ · ventilation (PEEP, long Te) · surfactant · iNO if PPHN

cards.q: PPV rate for a newborn, and when do you reassess?
cards.a:
PPV rate for a newborn, and when do you reassess?
40–60 breaths/min; reassess at 30 seconds.

cards.q: After 30 s of PPV the HR is 60–100. What next? Below 60?
cards.a:
After 30 s of PPV the HR is 60–100. What next? Below 60?
60–100: continue PPV
< 60: add compressions

cards.q: What is secondary apnea, and will stimulation restart breathing?
cards.a:
What is secondary apnea, and will stimulation restart breathing?
The final stop in breathing after primary apnea and weak gasping. HR and BP keep falling. Breathing won't return without PPV — stimulation doesn't work.

cards.q: Secondary apnea — how do the slide and the book differ?
cards.a:
Secondary apnea — how do the slide and the book differ?
The slide labels the gasping itself as secondary apnea; the book puts gasping just before it.

cards.q: Standard neonatal intubation: route, blade and tube?
cards.a:
Standard neonatal intubation: route, blade and tube?
Oral with a straight Miller blade (size 0 preterm, 1 term) and an uncuffed tube.

cards.q: Indications for neonatal intubation?
cards.a:
Indications for neonatal intubation?
Thick meconium in a non-vigorous baby, ineffective bag-mask, prolonged PPV, compressions, surfactant, diaphragmatic hernia.

cards.q: How do you confirm neonatal ETT placement, and how long can each attempt last?
cards.a:
How do you confirm neonatal ETT placement, and how long can each attempt last?
Bilateral breath sounds, CO₂ detector, CXR. Limit each attempt to 30 seconds.

cards.q: Other neonatal airway routes besides oral intubation?
cards.a:
Other neonatal airway routes besides oral intubation?
Oral or nasopharyngeal airways; nasal prongs for CPAP.

cards.q: Oral vs nasal intubation — what do the sources say?
cards.a:
Oral vs nasal intubation — what do the sources say?
Neither source compares them — get that from lecture.

cards.q: What are the signs of increased work of breathing in a newborn?
cards.a:
What are the signs of increased work of breathing in a newborn?
Tachypnea (> 60), grunting, retractions, nasal flaring, cyanosis.

cards.q: What is grunting, and why does the infant do it?
cards.a:
What is grunting, and why does the infant do it?
Closing the glottis on exhalation — creates back-pressure (self-made PEEP) that keeps alveoli open. Signals low lung volume.

cards.q: What causes retractions, and where are they seen?
cards.a:
What causes retractions, and where are they seen?
Stiff (low-compliance) lungs pulling the soft infant chest wall inward. Intercostal, substernal or suprasternal, graded mild to severe.

cards.q: Why does an infant nasal flare?
cards.a:
Why does an infant nasal flare?
To widen the nares, cut resistance and bring in more air.

cards.q: Name 5 causes of increased WOB in the newborn.
cards.a:
Name 5 causes of increased WOB in the newborn.
RDS (surfactant deficiency), TTN (retained lung fluid), pneumothorax/air leaks, pneumonia, MAS.

cards.q: Why are infants predisposed to respiratory distress?
cards.a:
Why are infants predisposed to respiratory distress?
Narrow airway, cartilaginous chest wall, low reserve, high metabolic rate.

cards.q: Does RDS raise or lower FRC — and what does the RDS slide say?
cards.a:
Does RDS raise or lower FRC — and what does the RDS slide say?
RDS lowers FRC — grunting is the attempt to raise it. The RDS slide lists "Increased FRC" — the opposite.

cards.q: What is the order of the neonatal physical exam?
cards.a:
What is the order of the neonatal physical exam?
Observe → history and gestational age (Dubowitz/Ballard) → AGA/SGA/LGA → quiet exam (color, respiration, activity) → hands-on → reflexes (rooting, suck, grasp, Moro)

cards.q: Neonatal normals: HR, RR, axillary temperature?
cards.a:
Neonatal normals: HR, RR, axillary temperature?
HR 120–160 · RR 30–60 · temp 36.2–37.3 °C (axillary)

cards.q: Define apnea in a newborn.
cards.a:
Define apnea in a newborn.
No breathing for > 15–20 seconds with cyanosis or bradycardia.

cards.q: Neonatal distress presentations, and first-line treatment?
cards.a:
Neonatal distress presentations, and first-line treatment?
Tachypnea, grunting, retractions, flaring, cyanosis, poor temperature control, limpness. O₂ first, then CPAP or ventilation.

cards.q: What does each finding suggest: scaphoid abdomen · shifted PMI · weak femoral pulses · bulging fontanelle?
cards.a:
What does each finding suggest: scaphoid abdomen · shifted PMI · weak femoral pulses · bulging fontanelle?
Scaphoid abdomen → diaphragmatic hernia
Shifted PMI → pneumothorax or atelectasis
Weak femoral pulses → coarctation
Bulging fontanelle → raised ICP

cards.q: Pediatric respiratory exam — what do you assess?
cards.a:
Pediatric respiratory exam — what do you assess?
Localize disease (auscultate, percuss, CXR), check gas exchange (ABG, SpO₂), and judge rate, depth, rhythm and ease.

cards.q: When does a child's resting respiratory rate need investigation?
cards.a:
When does a child's resting respiratory rate need investigation?
After age 1: RR > 40. After age 5: > 35.

cards.q: First-line treatment: RDS · MAS · TTN · epiglottitis · croup?
cards.a:
First-line treatment: RDS · MAS · TTN · epiglottitis · croup?
RDS → steroids, surfactant, ventilation
MAS → suction if not vigorous, O₂
TTN → O₂, CPAP
Epiglottitis → O₂, prepare to intubate
Croup → humidity, fluids, observation

cards.q: What are chest X-rays used for in neonatal/pediatric care?
cards.a:
What are chest X-rays used for in neonatal/pediatric care?
Confirm a diagnosis and localize disease · check tube and line placement · follow progression and response to therapy.

cards.q: Where should a neonatal ETT tip sit on CXR?
cards.a:
Where should a neonatal ETT tip sit on CXR?
Halfway between the carina and the clavicles.

cards.q: Specific conditions a CXR is used for?
cards.a:
Specific conditions a CXR is used for?
BPD, pneumomediastinum, pneumopericardium, foreign body.

cards.q: Normal heart rate by age: newborn/fetus, infant, children?
cards.a:
Normal heart rate by age: newborn/fetus, infant, children?
Newborn/fetus 120–160 · infant about 123–138 · about 80 at 5 years, about 70 at 10 years, 60s by 15 years

cards.q: Neonatal resuscitation heart-rate lines?
cards.a:
Neonatal resuscitation heart-rate lines?
> 100 is the goal · < 100 → PPV · < 60 → compressions

cards.q: Normal respiratory rate by age: newborn, infant, children?
cards.a:
Normal respiratory rate by age: newborn, infant, children?
Newborn 30–60 (> 60 = tachypnea, an RDS sign) · infant about 30 · about 22 at 5 years, 18–19 at 10–15 years

cards.q: Bradycardia cutoffs: fetal, newborn, and children by age?
cards.a:
Bradycardia cutoffs: fetal, newborn, and children by age?
Fetal < 100 · newborn < 100 · children: < 100 under 3 years · < 60 at 3–9 years · < 50 at 9–16 years

cards.q: Bradycardia in a child usually means what, and what do you do?
cards.a:
Bradycardia in a child usually means what, and what do you do?
Hypoxia — ventilate and oxygenate first. HR < 60 with poor perfusion → CPR.

cards.q: Fetal bradycardia most often signals what?
cards.a:
Fetal bradycardia most often signals what?
Asphyxia.

cards.q: Tachycardia cutoffs: fetal and newborn? Most common fetal cause?
cards.a:
Tachycardia cutoffs: fetal and newborn? Most common fetal cause?
Fetal > 180 — most often maternal fever (also β-agonist tocolytics)
Newborn > 160

cards.q: How is tachycardia in a child classified, and how is SVT treated?
cards.a:
How is tachycardia in a child classified, and how is SVT treated?
By QRS width. Narrow = sinus or SVT. SVT: vagal maneuvers → adenosine → cardioversion if unstable.

cards.q: How is the infant larynx different from an adult's?
cards.a:
How is the infant larynx different from an adult's?
Higher and more anterior; epiglottis larger, floppy, U-shaped.

cards.q: Narrowest point of the pediatric airway, and why it matters?
cards.a:
Narrowest point of the pediatric airway, and why it matters?
The cricoid — a little swelling causes major obstruction.

cards.q: Why use a straight blade and an uncuffed tube in infants?
cards.a:
Why use a straight blade and an uncuffed tube in infants?
Because the larynx is high and anterior and the airway is narrowest at the cricoid.

cards.q: What causes cyanosis, and at what level of desaturated Hb does it appear?
cards.a:
What causes cyanosis, and at what level of desaturated Hb does it appear?
Deoxygenated hemoglobin; appears at about 5 g/dL desaturated Hb — so hypoxemia may already be significant.

cards.q: Where do you check for central cyanosis, and is acrocyanosis normal?
cards.a:
Where do you check for central cyanosis, and is acrocyanosis normal?
On the trunk (mucous membranes in dark skin). Acrocyanosis (blue hands and feet) is normal after birth.

cards.q: Central cyanosis doesn't correct with 100% O₂. Suspect what?
cards.a:
Central cyanosis doesn't correct with 100% O₂. Suspect what?
A right-to-left shunt — PPHN or heart disease.

cards.q: Name 4 conditions where cyanosis is seen.
cards.a:
Name 4 conditions where cyanosis is seen.
PPHN, pneumothorax, apnea, Wilson-Mikity.

cards.q: Why is thermoregulation so important in newborns?
cards.a:
Why is thermoregulation so important in newborns?
They rely on brown fat — they can't shiver well.

cards.q: What is the thermoregulation goal, and the target rectal temperature?
cards.a:
What is the thermoregulation goal, and the target rectal temperature?
The neutral thermal environment (lowest O₂ consumption); rectal 36.5–37.5 °C.

cards.q: The 4 ways newborns lose heat — and the fix for each? Which is largest?
cards.a:
The 4 ways newborns lose heat — and the fix for each? Which is largest?
Evaporative → dry immediately
Radiant (largest) → cap, warm blanket, radiant warmer
Conductive → warm mattress and surfaces
Convective → avoid drafts, warm the gases

cards.q: Incubator vs radiant warmer — trade-offs?
cards.a:
Incubator vs radiant warmer — trade-offs?
Incubator: controlled and quiet but limits access
Radiant warmer: access, but harder to control and more water loss

cards.q: Hypothermia in pediatric patients — most common setting and concern?
cards.a:
Hypothermia in pediatric patients — most common setting and concern?
Mostly after trauma; CNS injury can stop shivering. Address it in the trauma survey; prevent it in burns.

cards.q: Why do RTs care about a cold infant?
cards.a:
Why do RTs care about a cold infant?
Cold causes acidosis, pulmonary vasoconstriction and hypoxemia — and blowing cold O₂ on the face causes heat loss.

cards.q: Define cold stress.
cards.a:
Define cold stress.
Any drop below the thermoneutral temperature.

cards.q: How does the newborn respond to cold?
cards.a:
How does the newborn respond to cold?
Norepinephrine → brown fat burned (nonshivering thermogenesis) → ↑ O₂ consumption, ↓ glucose.

cards.q: Trace the chain of consequences from cold stress to death.
cards.a:
Trace the chain of consequences from cold stress to death.
Peripheral vasoconstriction → anaerobic metabolism → metabolic acidosis → pulmonary vasoconstriction → hypoxemia → death if uncorrected

cards.q: Other consequences of cold stress?
cards.a:
Other consequences of cold stress?
Hypoglycemia, calories lost for growth, less surfactant, bradycardia and arrhythmias.

cards.q: What is insensible water loss?
cards.a:
What is insensible water loss?
Water lost by evaporation from the skin and respiratory tract.

cards.q: What increases insensible water loss?
cards.a:
What increases insensible water loss?
Prematurity (thin skin), small size, respiratory distress, high temperature, skin breakdown/open defects, radiant warmers and phototherapy, motor activity and crying.

cards.q: What decreases insensible water loss?
cards.a:
What decreases insensible water loss?
Humidity and heat shields.

cards.q: Why do children dehydrate faster?
cards.a:
Why do children dehydrate faster?
A larger BSA means more water loss.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: Who gets ROP, and what triggers it?
cards.a:
Who gets ROP, and what triggers it?
Premature babies (< 31 wk, ≤ 1250 g) plus oxygen. Formerly called retrolental fibroplasia.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: What is the pathway from high PaO₂ to blindness in ROP?
cards.a:
What is the pathway from high PaO₂ to blindness in ROP?
High PaO₂ → retinal vasoconstriction → vessel necrosis → abnormal new vessels → scar → retinal detachment

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: What are the 5 stages of ROP?
cards.a:
What are the 5 stages of ROP?
1 demarcation line · 2 ridge · 3 extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation · 4 partial detachment · 5 total detachment

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: How is ROP treated and prevented? Target PaO₂?
cards.a:
How is ROP treated and prevented? Target PaO₂?
Treat: cryotherapy or laser; vitrectomy/lensectomy late. Prevent: careful O₂ with monitoring, PaO₂ 50–70.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: What is NEC and who gets it?
cards.a:
What is NEC and who gets it?
Ischemia and necrosis of the intestine — mostly premature, formula-fed babies.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: What 3 factors cause NEC, and what protects against it?
cards.a:
What 3 factors cause NEC, and what protects against it?
(1) bowel wall ischemia (asphyxia, PDA, UAC, exchange transfusion) + (2) bacterial invasion + (3) formula feeding. Breast milk protects.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: Signs of NEC, and the classic X-ray finding?
cards.a:
Signs of NEC, and the classic X-ray finding?
Bloody (guaiac +) stools, abdominal distention, bilious residuals/vomiting, feeding intolerance. X-ray: pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall).

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: How is NEC treated?
cards.a:
How is NEC treated?
NPO, NG suction, IV nutrition, antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin), serial abdominal X-rays, surgery if perforated.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: What causes neonatal pneumothorax, and with which diseases is it more common?
cards.a:
What causes neonatal pneumothorax, and with which diseases is it more common?
Alveolar rupture → air in the pleural space. Mostly from mechanical ventilation (barotrauma); more common with RDS and MAS.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: Signs of pneumothorax in a newborn?
cards.a:
Signs of pneumothorax in a newborn?
Sudden ↑ distress, retractions, tachypnea → bradycardia, cyanosis, apnea, hypotension. Asymmetric chest rise and a shifted PMI.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: How is neonatal pneumothorax diagnosed?
cards.a:
How is neonatal pneumothorax diagnosed?
Transillumination; CXR shows air with no lung markings, mediastinum shifted away in tension.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: Pneumothorax treatment by severity? Chest tube suction?
cards.a:
Pneumothorax treatment by severity? Chest tube suction?
Small → observe · emergency → needle aspiration · ongoing leak → chest tube (suction −15 to −25 cm H₂O)

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: Safe ABG ranges for neonates and children?
cards.a:
Safe ABG ranges for neonates and children?
pH 7.35–7.45 (acceptable 7.30–7.50) · PaCO₂ 35–45 · HCO₃⁻ 22–26 · BE ±4 · PaO₂ neonate 50–70 / child 80–100

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: How do you identify respiratory vs metabolic acidosis?
cards.a:
How do you identify respiratory vs metabolic acidosis?
pH ↓ with PaCO₂ ↑ = respiratory · pH ↓ with HCO₃⁻ ↓ = metabolic (reverse for alkalosis). Then check whether the other value has compensated.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: Typical ABG picture in RDS?
cards.a:
Typical ABG picture in RDS?
Hypoxemia that responds poorly to O₂ + rising PaCO₂ + mixed respiratory and metabolic (lactic) acidosis.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: RDS ABG targets, and when do you intubate?
cards.a:
RDS ABG targets, and when do you intubate?
Targets: PaO₂ 50–80, PaCO₂ < 60, pH > 7.25. Intubate if PaCO₂ > 60 with pH < 7.25.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: Neonatal ABG sampling: preferred site, timing after vent changes, and capillary limits?
cards.a:
Neonatal ABG sampling: preferred site, timing after vent changes, and capillary limits?
UAC preferred · draw 15–30 min after vent changes · capillary OK for pH and PaCO₂, not PaO₂

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: What is PPHN?
cards.a:
What is PPHN?
Persistent fetal circulation — severe pulmonary vasoconstriction, so pulmonary pressure stays high and blood shunts right-to-left through the FO and DA.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: Causes of PPHN, and which babies does it usually affect?
cards.a:
Causes of PPHN, and which babies does it usually affect?
Asphyxia, MAS, sepsis, diaphragmatic hernia, cold, acidosis. Usually term babies.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: Signs of PPHN?
cards.a:
Signs of PPHN?
Cyanosis and tachypnea within hours of birth that don't improve with O₂; preductal PaO₂ higher than postductal.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: Tests for PPHN?
cards.a:
Tests for PPHN?
Hyperoxia test, pre/postductal PaO₂, hyperoxia-hyperventilation test, echocardiogram.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::07 Perinatal Lung Disease & Prematurity
cards.q: How is PPHN treated?
cards.a:
How is PPHN treated?
Normal temperature, fluids, glucose, BP · minimal handling · mechanical ventilation (HFV) · inhaled nitric oxide · ECMO as a last resort

cards.q: How do bacteria reach the neonate, and what rupture time greatly raises the risk?
cards.a:
How do bacteria reach the neonate, and what rupture time greatly raises the risk?
Maternal intestinal/genital flora (or poor aseptic technique) ascend the birth canal after rupture of membranes — > 24 h greatly raises risk — then enter the mouth, lungs, gut and bloodstream.

cards.q: The 2 main organisms in neonatal bacterial infection? Others?
cards.a:
The 2 main organisms in neonatal bacterial infection? Others?
Group B strep and E. coli. Also Listeria, Staph aureus, Klebsiella, H. influenzae.

cards.q: Signs of neonatal sepsis, including the WBC cutoffs?
cards.a:
Signs of neonatal sepsis, including the WBC cutoffs?
Respiratory distress, tachycardia, lethargy, poor feeding, temperature instability (hypothermia in preemies), WBC < 5000 or > 15,000.

cards.q: How is neonatal sepsis diagnosed and treated? When are mothers screened for GBS?
cards.a:
How is neonatal sepsis diagnosed and treated? When are mothers screened for GBS?
Specimen or blood culture; ampicillin + gentamicin. Mothers screened for GBS at 35–37 weeks.

cards.q: Which maternal infection greatly increases the risk of neonatal sepsis?
cards.a:
Which maternal infection greatly increases the risk of neonatal sepsis?
Chorioamnionitis.

cards.q: At what bilirubin level does jaundice appear?
cards.a:
At what bilirubin level does jaundice appear?
Above about 5 mg/dL.

cards.q: Physiologic vs pathologic causes of hyperbilirubinemia?
cards.a:
Physiologic vs pathologic causes of hyperbilirubinemia?
Physiologic: high RBC mass with short RBC life, immature liver
Pathologic: Rh/ABO incompatibility, hemorrhage, infection, infant of a diabetic mother, galactosemia, hypothyroidism, breast-feeding

cards.q: What 5 criteria make jaundice pathologic?
cards.a:
What 5 criteria make jaundice pathologic?
Appears in the first 24 h · indirect > 13 mg/dL (term) or > 15 (preterm) · rises > 5 mg/dL in 24 h · direct > 1.5 · lasts > 7 days (term) or > 14 days (preterm)

cards.q: What is kernicterus and what does it cause?
cards.a:
What is kernicterus and what does it cause?
Unconjugated bilirubin enters the brain → cerebral palsy and deafness.

cards.q: How is hyperbilirubinemia treated? Side effect of phototherapy?
cards.a:
How is hyperbilirubinemia treated? Side effect of phototherapy?
Phototherapy (blue light makes bilirubin water-soluble; increases water loss) · exchange transfusion for high levels · treat the cause

cards.q: What does TORCH stand for?
cards.a:
What does TORCH stand for?
Toxoplasmosis · Other (syphilis, HIV, coxsackievirus, varicella, parvovirus B19) · Rubella · Cytomegalovirus · Herpes simplex type 2

cards.q: Toxoplasmosis: source and effects on the baby?
cards.a:
Toxoplasmosis: source and effects on the baby?
Cat feces or raw meat; hydrocephalus, seizures, jaundice.

cards.q: Congenital rubella: effects and prevention?
cards.a:
Congenital rubella: effects and prevention?
Cataracts, heart defects, deafness. Prevented by vaccinating the mother.

cards.q: Congenital CMV: effects and treatment?
cards.a:
Congenital CMV: effects and treatment?
IUGR, liver damage, microcephaly, progressive hearing loss. Supportive care.

cards.q: Neonatal herpes simplex type 2: how acquired, how prevented, how treated?
cards.a:
Neonatal herpes simplex type 2: how acquired, how prevented, how treated?
From the birth canal; cesarean if the mother has active lesions; treated with acyclovir.

cards.q: Why are the TORCH infections grouped together?
cards.a:
Why are the TORCH infections grouped together?
They cross to the fetus/newborn and cause similar findings: IUGR, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, microcephaly.

cards.q: What is an ASD and which way does blood flow after birth?
cards.a:
What is an ASD and which way does blood flow after birth?
The foramen-ovale flap fails to cover the opening → blood flows between the atria, left-to-right after birth.

cards.q: Most common type of ASD?
cards.a:
Most common type of ASD?
Ostium secundum — often symptomless.

cards.q: PALS: which rhythms are shockable, and which are not?
cards.a:
PALS: which rhythms are shockable, and which are not?
Shockable: VF and pulseless VT → defibrillate
Non-shockable: asystole and PEA → CPR and epinephrine

cards.q: PALS pulseless arrest sequence?
cards.a:
PALS pulseless arrest sequence?
CPR with O₂ → check rhythm → shock if shockable, resume CPR immediately → recheck every 2 minutes → treat reversible causes

cards.q: Pediatric CPR: rate, depth, ratio, and breaths with an advanced airway?
cards.a:
Pediatric CPR: rate, depth, ratio, and breaths with an advanced airway?
≥ 100/min, depth ⅓ of the chest · 30:2 if not intubated · 1 breath every 6–8 s if intubated · IV or IO access

cards.q: Define SIDS.
cards.a:
Define SIDS.
Sudden, unexplained death during sleep of an infant under 1 year; diagnosed at autopsy.

cards.q: SIDS pattern: age, season, time, sex?
cards.a:
SIDS pattern: age, season, time, sex?
2–4 months, winter, at night, males more than females.

cards.q: SIDS risk factors — and the strongest?
cards.a:
SIDS risk factors — and the strongest?
Stomach sleeping, maternal smoking (strongest), prematurity/low birth weight, soft bedding, bed sharing.

cards.q: How is SIDS prevented?
cards.a:
How is SIDS prevented?
"Back to Sleep" (supine), a smoke-free home, firm bedding.

cards.q: SIDS sleep position — what does the slide say vs the book?
cards.a:
SIDS sleep position — what does the slide say vs the book?
The slide says "place infant in prone position"; the book says prone is the #1 risk and infants should sleep on their backs. Ask your instructor which they'll accept.

cards.q: Pediatric airway differences from an adult?
cards.a:
Pediatric airway differences from an adult?
Larger tongue · larger, floppy, U-shaped epiglottis · larynx higher and more anterior · narrowest at the cricoid · narrow trachea · mainstem bronchi with less angle (aspiration either side)

cards.q: Why does the infant diaphragm do most of the work of breathing?
cards.a:
Why does the infant diaphragm do most of the work of breathing?
Ribs and sternum are mostly cartilage, the thorax is unstable, and abdominal contents are large → low reserve.

cards.q: Infants are obligate ___ breathers.
cards.a:
Infants are obligate ___ breathers.
Nose breathers.

cards.q: Pediatric body differences that matter: BSA, water, metabolism?
cards.a:
Pediatric body differences that matter: BSA, water, metabolism?
Larger BSA (heat and water loss) · about 80% water · higher metabolic rate and O₂ need · immature skin and blood–brain barrier · large head

cards.q: Why does a child's larger BSA matter?
cards.a:
Why does a child's larger BSA matter?
More heat loss, more water loss, and a larger %BSA per injury.

cards.q: How is burn BSA estimated in children, and how big is the head at birth vs adult?
cards.a:
How is burn BSA estimated in children, and how big is the head at birth vs adult?
Age-adjusted chart (Rule of Nines is adult). Head is about 19% at birth vs 8% in the adult.

cards.q: Parkland formula?
cards.a:
Parkland formula?
4 mL × kg × %BSA; half in the first 8 hours.

cards.q: Epiglottitis: cause, age, signs, X-ray, treatment?
cards.a:
Epiglottitis: cause, age, signs, X-ray, treatment?
Bacterial (H. influenzae b), ages 2–6. Rapid onset, high fever, drooling, leaning forward. Thumb sign. O₂, keep calm, intubate in the OR.

cards.q: Croup: cause, location, age, signs, X-ray, treatment?
cards.a:
Croup: cause, location, age, signs, X-ray, treatment?
Viral, subglottic, 6 months–3 years. Cold first, then barky cough and stridor. Steeple sign. Humidity, fluids, observation; racemic epinephrine and steroids if worse.

cards.q: Foreign body aspiration: sign, diagnosis, removal?
cards.a:
Foreign body aspiration: sign, diagnosis, removal?
Sudden dry, hacking cough; diagnosed by X-ray; removed by bronchoscopy.

cards.q: Smoke/CO inhalation: treatment, and how is CO diagnosed?
cards.a:
Smoke/CO inhalation: treatment, and how is CO diagnosed?
Immediate O₂; watch for airway damage. CO is diagnosed by CO-oximetry, not pulse ox.

cards.q: Congenital upper-airway hazards: choanal atresia and Pierre Robin?
cards.a:
Congenital upper-airway hazards: choanal atresia and Pierre Robin?
Choanal atresia → oral airway or intubation
Pierre Robin → jaw too small; tongue blocks the airway

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: What is pica, and its risks?
cards.a:
What is pica, and its risks?
Eating non-food items (dirt, paint, hair). Risks: nutrient deficiency, lead poisoning.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: Anorexia vs bulimia nervosa?
cards.a:
Anorexia vs bulimia nervosa?
Anorexia: refusing to eat in pursuit of thinness
Bulimia: binge eating then purging — look for eroded tooth enamel

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: Who most commonly has anorexia and bulimia?
cards.a:
Who most commonly has anorexia and bulimia?
Adolescent girls, with a distorted body image and perfectionism.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: Name the pediatric developmental delays.
cards.a:
Name the pediatric developmental delays.
Global developmental delay (2+ areas) · autism spectrum disorder · ADHD (inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, combined) · Asperger's (higher functioning, normal intelligence)

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: Oppositional defiant disorder vs conduct disorder?
cards.a:
Oppositional defiant disorder vs conduct disorder?
ODD: chronic defiance and anger
Conduct disorder: aggression, cruelty, destruction, stealing

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: How is a child's neurobehavioral development assessed?
cards.a:
How is a child's neurobehavioral development assessed?
Language, fine and gross motor, personal-social and cognitive development; the neuro exam.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: OSA and behavior problems — which causes which, per the slide vs the book?
cards.a:
OSA and behavior problems — which causes which, per the slide vs the book?
The slide shows behavior problems "resulting in" OSA; the book says untreated OSA causes behavior and learning problems.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: Obstructive vs central apnea?
cards.a:
Obstructive vs central apnea?
Obstructive: no airflow despite breathing effort
Central: no effort

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: Main causes of pediatric OSA, and how common is it?
cards.a:
Main causes of pediatric OSA, and how common is it?
Enlarged tonsils and adenoids and obesity (also small jaw, large tongue). Affects 2–4% of children.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: How is pediatric OSA diagnosed and treated?
cards.a:
How is pediatric OSA diagnosed and treated?
Polysomnogram (sleep study). Tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy or nasal CPAP during sleep.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: Signs of OSA in a child?
cards.a:
Signs of OSA in a child?
Loud snoring, disrupted sleep, behavior and learning problems (can look like ADHD), bedwetting, poor growth, high blood pressure.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: Normal pH for neonates and children, and the acceptable range?
cards.a:
Normal pH for neonates and children, and the acceptable range?
Normal 7.35–7.45; acceptable 7.30–7.50. Below 7.35 = acidemia; above 7.45 = alkalemia.

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: Fetal scalp pH: normal, slight asphyxia, severe asphyxia?
cards.a:
Fetal scalp pH: normal, slight asphyxia, severe asphyxia?
> 7.25 normal · 7.20–7.24 slight · < 7.20 severe

cards.d: RCP 201::Quick Answers::10 Pediatric Assessment & Continuing Care
cards.q: What pH and PaCO₂ define ventilatory failure?
cards.a:
What pH and PaCO₂ define ventilatory failure?
pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ > 60
